title.en: Transport in plants: diffusion, osmosis, transpiration and translocation

text.en: A giant tree lifts water to a leaf over 50 metres above the ground, with no heart or pump. The plant does it with osmosis, evaporation and the cohesion of water.

Diffusion is the movement of molecules from higher to lower concentration without energy; imbibition is the swelling of dry solids such as seeds as they absorb water.
Active transport uses energy (ATP) and membrane proteins called pumps to move substances against a concentration gradient.
Osmosis is the movement of water from higher to lower water concentration through a semipermeable membrane; in a hypertonic solution a plant cell loses water and its protoplasm shrinks, called plasmolysis.
Root hairs are thin-walled extensions of epidermal cells that increase the surface area for absorbing water and minerals.
Water moves from the root hair across the cortex to the xylem by the apoplast pathway (through cell walls) or the symplast pathway (through cytoplasm and plasmodesmata); the Casparian strip forces water through the cells at the endodermis.
Transpiration is evaporation of water from aerial parts, mainly through stomata; guard cells open the stoma when turgid and close it when flaccid.
It creates the transpiration pull, supplies water for photosynthesis, cools the leaf and keeps cells turgid.
Water rises in the xylem by root pressure, capillary action, adhesion-cohesion of water molecules and transpiration pull, together called ascent of sap.
Minerals enter the root by active absorption using ATP; elements like N, P, S and K are remobilised to young leaves but calcium is not.
Phloem carries sucrose from a source such as a leaf to a sink such as a root or fruit by the pressure flow hypothesis, and the flow can be in both directions.

problem.en: A plant cell is placed in a strong salt solution. What happens and why?

why.en: It has a lower water concentration than the cell.

text.en: Water leaves the cell by osmosis.

why.en: Water moves from higher to lower concentration.

text.en: The protoplasm shrinks away from the cell wall, which is plasmolysis.

prompt.en: Explain how water reaches the top of a tall tree.

requiredIdeas.en: Root pressure pushes water up a little
Transpiration pull sucks the water column
Cohesion and adhesion keep the column unbroken

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking the roots pump water to the top like a motor

points.en: Diffusion and osmosis are passive; active transport needs ATP.
Water travels by apoplast or symplast pathways to xylem.
Transpiration pull, root pressure, capillarity and cohesion-adhesion cause the ascent of sap.
Phloem carries sucrose from source to sink by pressure flow.
